opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea behind Genie was that we wanted to learn an interactive environment, something you could actually take actions in, without having any action labels. That shaped the data question a lot. If you think about where the richest source of interactive experience lives, it's on the internet in the form of video. There are enormous amounts of people playing games, recording themselves doing things, and so on. But none of that comes with the actions attached. You see what happened on screen, but not which button was pressed.

So we deliberately chose to train only from videos, and then the model has to infer a latent action space on its own: what changed between frames that could be explained by some controllable action.

For the main model we focused on 2D platformer games. That was a pragmatic choice in a few ways. Platformers have a fairly consistent notion of control: there's usually a character you move left, right, jump, and so on. That gave us a domain that was diverse visually, with lots of different art styles, worlds, and mechanics, but still had a shared underlying structure of controllability. That made it a good testbed for whether the model could discover a consistent set of latent actions across very different-looking games.

Data quality turned out to matter a lot. When you scrape gameplay videos, you get menus, title screens, people's webcams in the corner, edited montages, and plenty of footage that isn't really gameplay at all. We started with a very large pool and did quite a bit of filtering to get down to clips that actually reflected someone playing. One of the lessons was that a smaller, cleaner dataset was more useful than just throwing everything in.

We also wanted to make sure the approach wasn't specific to games, so we trained a version on robotics video as well. There, too, we didn't use the action labels. It was encouraging that the model still learned meaningful, consistent latent actions and some sense of object dynamics and deformation.

So the overall philosophy was: lean into the scale and diversity of unlabeled video, pick domains where controllability is a meaningful concept, and invest in filtering so the model actually sees interaction rather than noise. The longer-term motivation is that if you can learn world models this way, you open the door to training agents in an essentially unlimited variety of generated environments.

r001.rationale: It cites visual variety and different mechanics as reasons for using platformers, but does not clearly identify diversity of behaviors as a reason.

r002.rationale: It states that a robotics-video version was trained without action labels.

r003.rationale: It says robotics training was meant to check that the approach was not specific to games, and reports learning meaningful latent actions and object dynamics from robotics video.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that was actually one of the first big decisions we had to make. The thing we really wanted with Genie was to learn a world model from unlabeled videos, so we weren't going to go collect action labels or anything like that. That was sort of the whole point. So the question became, where do you get a lot of video where there's some agent moving around and interacting with an environment in a way that's consistent enough to learn from?

And we landed on 2D platformer videos from the internet, which ended up being around 30,000 hours after filtering. The reason platformers were appealing is that they have this nice structure. There's usually a character, that character is controlled by someone, and the controls are reasonably consistent across games. You go left, you go right, you jump. So even though we never see the actions, there's a latent action space there that's fairly low-dimensional and shared across a lot of the data, and that's exactly what we were hoping the model could discover on its own.

The filtering was a big part of it, too. A lot of what you get when you scrape gameplay videos isn't what you want. There are menus, title screens, people talking over a webcam in the corner, and so on. So we trained a classifier to keep the clips that looked like actual gameplay and threw the rest out. That took the dataset down quite a bit, but the quality mattered more than the raw size.

And then the other thing we did, which I think was important for showing the idea was general, was to also train on robotics data, the RT-1 data, where there's a robot arm interacting with objects. That has a totally different visual distribution, but the same underlying story applies. There's an agent, there are actions driving what happens frame to frame, and we wanted to see if the latent action model would pick those up without any labels. And it did, which was really nice confirmation that this wasn't just a platformer trick.

r001.rationale: The response cites consistent controls shared across platformer games, but it does not identify diversity of behaviors as a reason for choosing them.

r002.rationale: It says they trained on RT-1 robotics data to test whether the latent action model could learn without labels, describing robot interaction video without action labels.

r003.rationale: It says the robotics data was used to show the idea was general beyond platformers, and describes a robot arm interacting with objects as the real-world setting.

astra-6.text:
The key question was whether we could learn from video without needing the actions that produced it. If you require action labels, that really limits the data you can use. With video, there’s the possibility of learning from a much broader set of experiences.

For Genie, we focused on videos of 2D platformer games. That gave us a useful setting for exploring the idea: you can see a character moving through an environment, and there’s a fairly clear relationship between what the character does and how the scene changes. But the model doesn’t get to see which buttons someone pressed. It has to learn that underlying structure from the video itself, and then make it something you can control.

r001.rationale: The response says video could provide a broader set of experiences, but does not identify diversity of behaviors as a reason for choosing 2D platformer videos.

r002.rationale: It describes 2D platformer videos without button labels; it does not say Genie was trained on robotics observations without associated actions.

r003.rationale: The response gives no robotics-data training purpose or claim about applicability to real-world environments.

sol-6.1.text:
We wanted to explore whether we could learn an interactive environment from video alone, without having access to the actions that generated it. That’s important because there’s so much video available, whereas collecting data with action labels is much more restrictive.

For Genie, we focused on videos of 2D platformer games. That gave us a relatively constrained setting, but still a lot of diversity in characters, environments, and movement. The model had to infer the underlying actions just by observing how things changed between frames. So the choice was really about balancing diversity with a setting where we could study whether that approach actually worked.

r001.rationale: The response says platformer videos offered diversity in characters, environments, and movement, and cites balancing diversity as a reason for the choice.

r002.rationale: It describes training from game videos without action labels; it does not say the observations were robotics data.

r003.rationale: It does not state that robotics data was used to demonstrate applicability to real-world environments.
